items.stem: Define the term 'misrepresentation'.
items.answer: An untrue statement of fact (not opinion or intention) made by one party to the other before the contract, which induces the other party to enter into the contract.

items.stem: Hana bought an antique clock from Yusuf, a dealer, for $20 000 after Yusuf said it was made by a famous artist. Yusuf relied on an old catalogue without checking. The statement was untrue. Advise Hana which type of misrepresentation has occurred and what remedies are available.
items.answer: Law: fraudulent: knowingly, without belief or recklessly (Derry v Peek); negligent under s2(1) MA 1967: liable unless reasonable grounds for belief proved (Howard Marine v Ogden); damages on fraud basis (Royscot); innocent: reasonable grounds; rescission or damages in lieu under s2(2). Application: the statement that it was made by a famous artist was a false statement of fact that induced the sale; Yusuf relied on an old catalogue without checking, so the misrepresentation is negligent under s2(1) MA 1967, as Yusuf cannot show reasonable grounds (Howard Marine). Conclusion: The misrepresentation is negligent under s2(1) MA 1967, as Yusuf cannot show reasonable grounds (Howard Marine).

items.stem: Amara bought a hair salon in Lagos from Ines. Before the sale Ines said that the business made a profit of $50 000 a year. In fact it had made a loss for two years. Amara relied on the statement. Amara has just found out the truth after two weeks. Advise Amara on whether there has been an actionable misrepresentation and what remedies are available. Explain the relevant law, apply it to the facts and evaluate the strength of any arguments available.
items.answer: Law: a misrepresentation is a false statement of fact which induces the contract; opinions are not usually statements of fact (Bisset v Wilkinson) unless made by an expert (Esso v Mardon); types: fraudulent (Derry v Peek), negligent under s2(1) MA 1967 (Howard Marine), innocent; rescission may be barred by affirmation or lapse of time (Long v Lloyd; Leaf v International Galleries); damages under s2(1) on the fraud measure (Royscot). Application: Ines's statement was a false statement of fact; Amara relied on it, so inducement is satisfied (Redgrave v Hurd); Amara has just found out the truth after two weeks, which affects whether rescission is still available. Conclusion: If the statement was a false statement of fact, Amara can probably claim damages under s2(1) MA 1967; rescission depends on whether it is barred by delay or affirmation.

items.stem: Freya agreed to buy a painting in a warehouse from Priya for $15 000. Unknown to both of them, it was worth much less than both believed. Advise Freya whether the contract is valid.
items.answer: Law: common mistake as to the existence of the subject matter makes the contract void (Couturier v Hastie); a mistake as to quality does not, unless the subject matter is essentially different (Bell v Lever Bros; Great Peace Shipping). Application: both parties shared the mistake; the mistake was that it was worth much less than both believed, which is a mistake as to quality, which does not usually make the contract void (Bell v Lever Bros). Conclusion: The position is a mistake as to quality, which does not usually make the contract void (Bell v Lever Bros).

items.stem: Explain the difference between common, mutual and unilateral mistake.
items.answer: Common: both parties make the same fundamental mistake (Couturier v Hastie); mutual: they are at cross-purposes (Raffles v Wichelhaus); unilateral: one party is mistaken and the other knows or ought to know (Cundy v Lindsay; Hartog).

items.stem: Arjun sold a car by email and a written finance agreement to a rogue, Tariq, who claimed to be a respected doctor. Tariq paid with a worthless cheque and sold the car to Mateo, an innocent buyer. Advise Arjun whether Arjun can recover the car from Mateo. In your answer, refer to decided cases and assess how a court is likely to decide.
items.answer: Law: a mistake as to identity may make a contract void if identity is crucial (Cundy v Lindsay); face to face there is a presumption of an intention to deal with the person present, so the contract is voidable for fraud (Phillips v Brooks; Lewis v Averay); written contracts identify the parties by the document (Shogun Finance v Hudson); a third party in good faith acquires title under a voidable contract not yet rescinded. Application: Arjun sold a car by email and a written finance agreement to Tariq; this was at a distance/in writing, so the contract was probably void (Cundy v Lindsay; Shogun Finance); so Mateo must return it to Arjun. Conclusion: Mateo must return it to Arjun.

items.stem: Tomás, aged 72, agreed to guarantee a large business loan for Samuel's company after advice from Samuel, Tomás's nephew, who managed Tomás's affairs. Tomás did not receive independent advice. The transaction was very much to Tomás's disadvantage. Advise Tomás whether the transaction can be set aside.
items.answer: Law: undue influence may be actual (BCCI v Aboody) or presumed where there is a relationship of trust and confidence and a transaction that calls for explanation (Etridge); some relationships are presumed (e.g. solicitor and client); others must be proved (Lloyds Bank v Bundy); the presumption can be rebutted, e.g. by independent advice; the remedy is rescission. Application: Samuel is Tomás's nephew, who managed Tomás's affairs, which suggests trust and confidence; the transaction calls for explanation as it is very disadvantageous; no independent advice was given. Conclusion: Undue influence is likely to be presumed, so the transaction can probably be set aside.

items.stem: Explain why the courts distinguish between face-to-face dealings and contracts made at a distance when the mistake is about identity.
items.answer: At a distance the identity of the named person is usually crucial, so the contract may be void (Cundy v Lindsay; Shogun Finance); face to face, the seller is presumed to intend to contract with the person present, so it is only voidable for fraud (Phillips v Brooks; Lewis v Averay), protecting innocent third parties.

items.answer: Law: undue influence may be actual (BCCI v Aboody) or presumed where there is a relationship of trust and confidence and a transaction that calls for explanation (Etridge); some relationships are presumed (e.g. solicitor and client); others must be proved (Lloyds Bank v Bundy); the presumption can be rebutted, e.g. by independent advice; the remedy is rescission. Application: Tariq is Aisha's carer, on whom Aisha relied completely, which suggests trust and confidence; the transaction calls for explanation as it is very disadvantageous; no independent advice was given. Conclusion: Undue influence is likely to be presumed, so the transaction can probably be set aside.

items.stem: Identify one way in which a restraint in an employment contract differs from a restraint on the seller of a business.
items.answer: Employment restraints are treated more strictly because of unequal bargaining power.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a valid difference; 1 mark: both sides made clear, e.g. employment restraints are treated more strictly because of unequal bargaining power; sale of business restraints protect goodwill paid for and may be wider (Nordenfelt). [2]

items.stem: Explain the approach to illegality set out in Patel v Mirza (2016).
items.answer: The court asks whether enforcing the claim would harm the integrity of the legal system, considering the purpose of the law that was broken, other relevant public policies, and whether denying the claim would be proportionate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each factor. [3]

items.stem: Zara worked as a hairdresser for Ethan Ltd in Riyadh. The contract said that after leaving, Zara would not work in the same trade anywhere in the country for ten years. Zara has left and set up a competing business. State, with a brief reason, the most likely legal outcome.
items.answer: The clause is probably void as wider than necessary (Mason v Provident). Reason: restraints are prima facie void unless reasonable (Nordenfelt)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct outcome (the clause is probably void as wider than necessary (Mason v Provident)). 1 mark: reason based on the rule, e.g. restraints are prima facie void unless reasonable (Nordenfelt). [2]
